content_units: Roth IRA vs Traditional IRA at Age 29
For a 29-year-old single filer earning   $78,000   in the U.S., both accounts are strong retirement tools, but they work very differently on taxes and flexibility.
The short version:
-   Roth IRA  : pay tax now, qualified withdrawals later are tax-free.
-   Traditional IRA  : possible tax break now, withdrawals later are taxed as ordinary income.
- For your goal of   long-term growth plus flexibility during early career changes  , a   Roth IRA is often the cleaner fit  .
Plain-English Comparison Table
Feature   Roth IRA   Traditional IRA   What it means for you
Contributions   Made with after-tax money   Usually made with pre-tax or tax-deductible money if eligible   Roth gives no upfront tax break; Traditional may lower current taxable income
Tax on growth   Tax-free if rules are met   Tax-deferred until withdrawal   Roth is usually better if you expect higher future tax rates
Tax on retirement withdrawals   Usually tax-free   Taxed as ordinary income   Roth creates more predictable retirement income

Early access to contributions   You can generally withdraw your contributions anytime, tax- and penalty-free   Early withdrawals can trigger tax and a 10% penalty unless an exception applies   Roth offers more flexibility if life or career plans change
Required minimum distributions   None during your lifetime   Yes, generally starting in later retirement years   Roth gives more control over timing

Income limits for contributing   Yes, Roth has income limits   No income limit to contribute, but deduction rules may limit tax benefit   At $78,000 single, Roth contribution eligibility is generally still available
Best fit   People wanting tax-free retirement income and flexibility   People wanting a current-year tax deduction   Your stated priorities lean Roth
Tax Tradeoffs for Your Situation
Why Roth IRA stands out
- At   $78,000 salary  , you are likely in a   moderate tax bracket  , not an ultra-high one.
- That often makes it reasonable to   pay tax now   and lock in   tax-free withdrawals later  .
- Since you want   long-term retirement savings  , decades of tax-free growth can be very valuable.
- Since you also want   flexibility for early career changes  , Roth is friendlier because you can generally pull out your   contributed principal   without tax or penalty.
When a Traditional IRA may be better
- If you strongly value a   tax deduction this year  .
- If you expect to be in a   meaningfully lower tax bracket in retirement  .
- If cash flow is tight and lowering current taxable income matters more than future flexibility.
Important practical note

If you are covered by a workplace retirement plan like a   401(k)  , the   Traditional IRA contribution may not be fully deductible   at your income level. That can reduce its appeal compared with a Roth IRA. Since you asked for a simple comparison and didn’t specify workplace-plan coverage, this is the main caveat to keep in mind.
Best Fit for Long-Term Savings and Career Flexibility
Likely recommendation: Roth IRA
A Roth IRA is usually the better choice here because it matches your priorities in order:
-   Long-term retirement savings  : tax-free growth and tax-free qualified withdrawals are powerful at age 29.
-   Flexibility  : contributions are more accessible if your career path changes, you go back to school, start a business, or face a gap between jobs.
-   Simplicity  : you know the tax was paid up front, so retirement planning is easier.
Trade-off alternative: Traditional IRA
Choose Traditional instead if:
- your main goal is   reducing taxes this year  , and
- you are   eligible for the deduction  , and
- you believe your retirement tax rate will likely be lower.
Simple Choosing Rule
Use this rule of thumb:
-   Choose Roth IRA   if you are early in your career, expect income to rise over time, want flexibility, and can afford to skip the current-year deduction.
-   Choose Traditional IRA   if you need the tax break now and are confident that deduction is available and more valuable than future tax-free withdrawals.
An even simpler version:
-   Roth = better for flexibility and future tax-free money
-   Traditional = better for a tax break now
Context for This Recommendation
This answer assumes:
- you are a   U.S. taxpayer filing single
- your income is approximately   $78,000 in salary
- you have   no existing IRA balance
- you want to optimize for   long-term saving first   and   career-change flexibility second
If those facts stay true,   Roth IRA is the default winner   for your stated goals.
